option_description: The data classification label applied to the session token store (database, cache, or file system) as documented in the data inventory or system configuration. Controls which downstream security controls (encryption, access logging, retention limits) are applied to the store.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `misclassification_as_non_sensitive` whenever this label is 'public' or 'internal', regardless of whether encryption or logging are also absent. A misclassified store inherits an inadequate control tier: encryption may not be mandated, access logging may be omitted, and retention limits may not be enforced. This single misconfiguration cascades into multiple downstream failures because policy engines, backup tools, and access-control systems inherit the wrong sensitivity tier.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Open the organization's data governance or CMDB tool (e.g., Collibra, Alation, ServiceNow CMDB). Search for the token store asset by name or connection string. Review the 'Data Classification' or 'Sensitivity' field on the asset record.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Collibra: Data Catalog → Search → [token store name] → Asset Detail → Classification tag | ServiceNow: CMDB → CI record → Data Classification field
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A label of 'confidential', 'restricted', or 'secret' for a session token store. Labels of 'public' or 'internal' indicate misclassification.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect infrastructure-as-code definitions (Terraform, CloudFormation, Helm values) for the token store resource. Look for classification or tag blocks applied to the resource.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn -E '(classification|data_sensitivity|sensitivity|data_class)' ./infra/ --include='*.tf' --include='*.yaml' --include='*.json'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A tag or label key such as `data_classification = "restricted"` on the Redis cluster, RDS instance, or S3 bucket backing the token store.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the cloud provider's tagging API to retrieve the classification tag on the token store resource directly.
how_to_obtain.command: aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources --tag-filters Key=Name,Values=<token-store-name> --query 'ResourceTagMappingList[].Tags' | jq '.[] | select(.Key=="data_classification")'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output containing `{"Key": "data_classification", "Value": "restricted"}` or equivalent. Absence of the tag or a value of 'public'/'internal' is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the data governance or platform security team to confirm whether a formal classification review was performed for this token store and review the signed-off classification record in the data inventory.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented classification decision dated within the last review cycle, with approval from the data owner, showing the store is labeled 'confidential', 'restricted', or 'secret'.

option_description: Indicates whether the session token store has encryption at rest enabled across both the primary store and all backup or export paths. A value of false if either the primary store or any backup destination is unencrypted.
security_impact: The Rego policy `unencrypted_token_at_rest` fires when `encryption_at_rest_enabled` is false even if a field- or volume-level encryption mode is declared, meaning the encryption declaration is only meaningful when this flag confirms it is active. Additionally, `misclassification_as_non_sensitive` includes a branch that fires when the store is misclassified AND encryption is absent, reinforcing that classification and encryption are jointly assessed. An unencrypted token store means any actor with read access to the storage medium obtains directly usable credentials without further cryptographic effort.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS RDS, check the StorageEncrypted attribute on the DB instance. For ElastiCache Redis, verify the at-rest encryption flag on the replication group.
how_to_obtain.command: aws rds describe-db-instances --query 'DBInstances[?DBInstanceIdentifier==`<instance-id>`].StorageEncrypted' && aws elasticache describe-replication-groups --replication-group-id <group-id> --query 'ReplicationGroups[].AtRestEncryptionEnabled'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: `true` returned for both commands. `false` or missing field is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Terraform or CloudFormation, locate the token store resource block and verify the encryption setting is present and set to true.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -A5 -B5 'storage_encrypted\|at_rest_encryption_enabled\|kms_key_id\|SSESpecification' ./infra/**/*.tf ./infra/**/*.yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: `storage_encrypted = true` and a `kms_key_id` reference for RDS; `at_rest_encryption_enabled = true` for ElastiCache. Absence or `false` is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the AWS Console, navigate to the token store service, open the instance or cluster, and inspect the encryption configuration tab.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console → RDS → Databases → [instance] → Configuration tab → Storage Encrypted | AWS Console → ElastiCache → Redis clusters → [cluster] → Description tab → Encryption at rest
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Field shows 'Yes' or 'Enabled'. 'No' or 'Disabled' is a finding. Repeat inspection for associated snapshot/backup destinations (S3 bucket SSE, EBS snapshot encryption).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify backup destinations also have encryption enabled. For S3-backed backups, check default bucket encryption and any per-object SSE settings.
how_to_obtain.command: aws s3api get-bucket-encryption --bucket <backup-bucket-name> && aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket <backup-bucket-name> | jq '.Policy' | python3 -m json.tool | grep -i 'deny\|ssl\|encrypt'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response shows `SSEAlgorithm: aws:kms` or `AES256`. A bucket with no default encryption rule or a policy that does not deny unencrypted puts is a finding.

option_description: Whether read and write access to the session token store is logged, providing an audit trail of all interactions with authentication credentials. Covers database query logs, Redis keyspace notifications or audit proxies, and OS-level file audit rules depending on store type.
security_impact: The Rego policy `misclassification_as_non_sensitive` includes a branch that fires when the store is misclassified AND access logging is absent. Without an access log, there is no forensic trail to detect bulk token extraction, unauthorized reads, or credential stuffing attacks against the store directly. For a high-sensitivity asset like a session token store, access logging is a baseline detective control required at the 'confidential' classification tier and above.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS RDS (MySQL/PostgreSQL), check if the audit or general query log is enabled via parameter group settings.
how_to_obtain.command: aws rds describe-db-parameters --db-parameter-group-name <param-group> --query 'Parameters[?ParameterName==`general_log` || ParameterName==`log_statement` || ParameterName==`pgaudit.log`].[ParameterName,ParameterValue]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: `general_log = 1` for MySQL or `log_statement = all` and `pgaudit.log = ddl,read,write` for PostgreSQL. All disabled or set to 'none' is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Redis, check if keyspace notifications are configured (a basic proxy for access events) or if an audit sidecar is deployed alongside the cache.
how_to_obtain.command: redis-cli -h <redis-host> -p 6379 CONFIG GET notify-keyspace-events && kubectl get pods -n <namespace> -l app=redis-audit-proxy --no-headers | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-empty keyspace notification config (e.g., `KEA`) or at least one audit proxy pod running. Empty config and zero proxy pods is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For file-system-backed token stores, check OS-level auditd rules to confirm read/write syscalls on the token file path are captured.
how_to_obtain.command: auditctl -l | grep -E '(token|session|auth)' && grep -rn 'token\|session' /etc/audit/rules.d/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An audit rule matching the token file path with `-p rwxa` flags present. No matching rules is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For cloud-managed token stores, verify that CloudTrail data events or equivalent are capturing API-level reads and writes to the store.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console → CloudTrail → Trails → [trail name] → Data events tab → Verify S3 or DynamoDB data events include the token store resource ARN
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Data event logging shows 'Read' and 'Write' enabled for the specific token store resource ARN. Absent or limited to management events only is a finding.

option_description: The number of days session tokens or their records are retained in the token store and backups before being purged. A value of -1 indicates no defined retention limit, meaning tokens accumulate indefinitely.
security_impact: The Rego policy `misclassification_as_non_sensitive` includes a branch that fires when the store is misclassified AND the retention policy is -1 (undefined). An undefined or excessively long retention period means expired credentials persist as dormant but potentially replayable tokens. Combined with the `token_persistence_beyond_session_lifetime` rule, which fires when `token_retention_policy_enforced` is false, a missing retention definition is the prerequisite failure that makes enforcement impossible.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the formal data retention policy document for the authentication system. Confirm a specific day count is defined for session tokens and that the policy has been approved and is current.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A policy document specifying a retention limit of 30, 90, or at most 365 days for session tokens, with a documented review date. Absence of any document or a value of 'indefinite' is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Redis-based token stores, inspect the default TTL configuration and check whether keys have TTLs assigned. Sample active token keys to verify TTL is set.
how_to_obtain.command: redis-cli -h <redis-host> CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy && redis-cli -h <redis-host> TTL <sample-session-key> && redis-cli -h <redis-host> OBJECT IDLETIME <sample-session-key>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: TTL returns a positive integer (seconds remaining). A return value of -1 (no TTL set) indicates tokens persist indefinitely and is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For database-backed token stores, inspect scheduled purge jobs or TTL columns to determine the effective retention period.
how_to_obtain.command: mysql -h <db-host> -u <user> -p -e "SHOW CREATE TABLE sessions;" && crontab -l | grep -i 'purge\|expire\|clean\|token' && systemctl list-timers | grep -i 'token\|session\|purge'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A TTL column with a configured interval, or a cron/systemd timer that runs a purge job. Absence of any purge mechanism or TTL column is a finding. Record the interval in days.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check application configuration files or environment variables for token lifetime and retention settings.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn -E '(TOKEN_TTL|SESSION_LIFETIME|TOKEN_EXPIRY|token.retention|session.expiry)' /etc/app/ /opt/app/config/ .env* --include='*.yaml' --include='*.conf' --include='*.env'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A variable such as `TOKEN_TTL=86400` (seconds) or `token.retention.days=30`. Absence of any retention-related variable is a finding. Convert seconds to days for the attribute value.

option_description: Whether the system automatically purges or expires stored tokens (in databases, caches, audit logs, and backup tables) after their validity window closes. True only when a technical mechanism — TTL, scheduled job, or eviction policy — actively removes tokens across all stores.
security_impact: The Rego policy `token_persistence_beyond_session_lifetime` fires directly when `token_retention_policy_enforced` is false. A defined policy without enforcement (e.g., a policy document exists but no purge job runs) is treated the same as no policy. Expired tokens that remain in storage become dormant credentials that can be replayed if signing secrets rotate or revocation checks are bypassed. This attribute must be true across all stores including primary DB, cache, and audit/log tables.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that Redis token keys are configured with TTL expiry and that no keys exist without a TTL in the session keyspace.
how_to_obtain.command: redis-cli -h <redis-host> --scan --pattern 'session:*' | head -20 | xargs -I{} redis-cli -h <redis-host> TTL {} | sort -n | head -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All sampled keys return positive TTL values. Any key returning -1 (persistent) indicates enforcement is incomplete and the attribute should be recorded as false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify the database purge job is scheduled, enabled, and has run successfully within its expected interval.
how_to_obtain.command: systemctl status token-purge.timer && journalctl -u token-purge.service --since '7 days ago' | grep -E '(Success|Deleted|Purged|rows)' && mysql -h <db-host> -u <user> -p -e "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < NOW();"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Timer status is 'active', journal shows recent successful runs with rows deleted, and the query returns 0 or a negligible count of expired rows. A non-zero expired-row count or inactive timer is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the application or framework session configuration to confirm automatic expiry is enabled, not just defined.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn -E '(session.cleanup|purge_on_expiry|auto_expire|gc_probability|gc_divisor|SESSION_CLEANUP)' /etc/app/ /opt/app/ --include='*.yaml' --include='*.php' --include='*.conf'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A setting like `session.cleanup = true` or `gc_probability = 1` with `gc_divisor = 100` confirming active garbage collection. Disabled or probability set to 0 is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review runbook or operational procedures to confirm a human or automated process is responsible for enforcing retention on audit/log tables and backup stores, not just the primary token store.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A runbook step or automation pipeline that explicitly covers purging tokens from audit log tables and backup snapshots, with evidence of recent execution. Coverage of primary store only is an incomplete finding.

option_description: Whether revoked tokens are actively removed from blacklists or revocation stores once their original expiry time has passed. Addresses the secondary accumulation problem where a revocation list itself becomes an unbounded store of expired credentials if not periodically pruned.
security_impact: The Rego policy `token_persistence_beyond_session_lifetime` fires when `revoked_token_store_cleanup_enabled` is false. A revocation list that is never pruned grows indefinitely and, while entries are 'revoked', they remain as recoverable credential data. If the revocation store is breached or the validation logic is bypassed, those entries represent replayable tokens. Additionally, bloated revocation lists degrade revocation check performance, creating operational pressure to disable checks entirely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Redis-based revocation blacklists, verify that revoked token entries are stored with TTL set to the token's original expiry time, not persisted indefinitely.
how_to_obtain.command: redis-cli -h <redis-host> --scan --pattern 'revoked:*' | head -20 | xargs -I{} redis-cli -h <redis-host> TTL {} | sort -n | head -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All sampled revoked token keys return positive TTL values corresponding approximately to the remaining time until original expiry. Keys returning -1 indicate no TTL and is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For database-backed revocation tables, verify a scheduled job or SQL event deletes rows where the original expiry timestamp has passed.
how_to_obtain.command: mysql -h <db-host> -u <user> -p -e "SHOW EVENTS LIKE '%revok%'; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM token_blacklist WHERE expires_at < NOW();" && crontab -l | grep -i 'blacklist\|revok'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A scheduled event or cron job targeting the blacklist table, and a COUNT of 0 or minimal expired rows. A large count of past-expiry rows and no cleanup job is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the token revocation service configuration for cleanup or TTL settings.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn -E '(revocation.cleanup|blacklist.ttl|revoked.expiry|REVOCATION_CLEANUP|blacklist_purge)' /etc/app/ /opt/app/ --include='*.yaml' --include='*.conf' --include='*.env'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A setting such as `revocation.cleanup.enabled: true` or `blacklist.ttl: 3600`. Absence of cleanup configuration is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the authentication platform team to confirm whether revocation store maintenance is part of the operational runbook and whether it has been executed recently.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A runbook section covering revocation list pruning with a defined schedule (e.g., daily) and evidence of recent execution in the change log or job history. No defined procedure is a finding.

option_description: The maximum number of days session tokens are retained in any persistent store beyond their expiry or revocation timestamp. Calculated as the worst-case lag across all stores including primary database, cache, audit tables, and backup archives. A value of 0 means tokens are removed at or before expiry.
security_impact: The Rego policy `token_persistence_beyond_session_lifetime` fires directly when `max_token_retention_days` is greater than 0. Any positive value indicates a window during which an expired or revoked token exists in storage and could be recovered and replayed. The severity scales with the value: a 1-day lag is a minor operational gap, while a 90-day lag in backup archives represents a long-lived exposure window that survives multiple key rotations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the primary token store for the oldest expired token record to determine actual retention lag in the live database.
how_to_obtain.command: mysql -h <db-host> -u <user> -p -e "SELECT DATEDIFF(NOW(), expires_at) AS days_past_expiry FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < NOW() ORDER BY expires_at ASC LIMIT 1;" 2>/dev/null || psql -h <db-host> -U <user> -c "SELECT EXTRACT(DAY FROM NOW() - expires_at) AS days_past_expiry FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < NOW() ORDER BY expires_at ASC LIMIT 1;"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A value of 0 or null (no expired rows found). Any positive integer indicates tokens are persisting past expiry; use this as the candidate max_token_retention_days value.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check backup retention settings to determine the longest-lived copy of token data. AWS RDS automated backup retention period represents the worst-case backup retention window.
how_to_obtain.command: aws rds describe-db-instances --query 'DBInstances[?DBInstanceIdentifier==`<instance-id>`].[DBInstanceIdentifier,BackupRetentionPeriod]' && aws elasticache describe-replication-groups --replication-group-id <group-id> --query 'ReplicationGroups[].SnapshotRetentionLimit'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Backup retention of 7 days is common. Use the maximum of this value and any live-store lag as the attribute value. A retention period of 0 for backups means no automated backups (verify manual snapshots separately).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect S3 lifecycle policies on backup buckets to determine how long token store exports or snapshots are retained.
how_to_obtain.command: aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket <backup-bucket> | jq '.Rules[] | {id: .ID, expiration: .Expiration, prefix: .Filter.Prefix}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lifecycle rules showing expiration in days (e.g., `{"expiration": {"Days": 30}}`). Absence of lifecycle rules means objects are retained indefinitely; record this as 36500 (no limit).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the backup and disaster recovery runbook to identify all persistent copies of token data (snapshots, exports, log archives) and their retention schedules. Use the longest retention period across all locations as the attribute value.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented inventory of all backup locations with explicit retention periods. The maximum value across all locations is the correct attribute value. An undocumented backup location or 'indefinite' retention is a finding.

option_description: Whether raw session token values (signed JWTs, opaque tokens, session IDs) are written in cleartext to application logs, audit trails, error reports, or monitoring pipelines. Detected through log pattern analysis, code review, or SAST tooling.
security_impact: The Rego policy `token_persistence_beyond_session_lifetime` fires when this is true because logs are persistent stores with their own (often longer) retention periods, extending token exposure beyond the session lifetime. The policy `token_exposure_in_log_and_audit_data` also fires when this is true and log masking is absent or log access is broader than the session store. Logs are typically subject to looser access controls than the primary token store, meaning log consumers, SIEM operators, and backup admins gain unintended access to live credentials.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search application log files and log aggregation systems (Splunk, ELK, CloudWatch Logs) for patterns matching JWT structure or opaque token formats that may have been written by the application.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn -E '(eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}|Bearer [A-Za-z0-9_\-\.]{20,}|Authorization: [A-Za-z0-9_\-\.]{20,}|session=[A-Za-z0-9]{20,})' /var/log/app/ /var/log/nginx/ --include='*.log' | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No matches. Any match containing a full token value (JWT or opaque) in a log line is a finding. Partial matches showing only token prefixes or hashes are acceptable.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use a SAST tool or grep-based code scan to identify logging statements that include session token variables, Authorization headers, or cookie values.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn -E '(log\.(info|debug|warn|error|trace).*token|log.*Authorization|log.*session_id|log.*Set-Cookie|logger\.(log|write).*Bearer)' ./src/ ./app/ --include='*.py' --include='*.js' --include='*.java' --include='*.go' --include='*.rb' | grep -v '#\|//' | head -30
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No matches. Any log statement that passes a token variable, Authorization header, or session cookie value directly to a logger is a finding. Check that log arguments are masked or redacted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the log aggregation system API for recent token-pattern matches across all ingested log sources.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <splunk-token>' 'https://<splunk-host>:8089/services/search/jobs' -d 'search=search index=app_logs earliest=-24h | regex _raw="eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}\\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}\." | head 10' -d 'output_mode=json' | jq '.results'
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Search & Reporting → Search bar → `index=app_logs earliest=-24h | regex _raw="eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}"` | ELK: Kibana → Discover → Filter by index pattern → KQL: `message: /eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}/`
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zero results. Any log event containing a full JWT or token string is a finding. Confirm the search covers all log sources including API gateway, application, and audit logs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect middleware or framework logging configuration to confirm token-related fields are explicitly excluded or masked before being passed to the logger.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn -E '(log_filter|sanitize|redact|mask|exclude.*token|exclude.*auth|filter_param)' ./config/ ./middleware/ --include='*.yaml' --include='*.rb' --include='*.py' --include='*.conf' | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A filter rule explicitly matching 'Authorization', 'token', 'session', or 'Set-Cookie' fields and replacing them with '[FILTERED]' or '[REDACTED]'. Absence of any such filter when token variables are used in log calls is a finding.

option_description: Controls the encryption method applied to session tokens at rest in the primary token store (database, cache, or session store). Determines whether tokens are stored as plaintext, hashed, field-level encrypted, volume-encrypted, or both field and volume encrypted.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'Unencrypted Token At Rest' exposure (score 8, high criticality) when this value is 'none' or 'hashed', since both expose usable token material to any actor with storage-level read access. Even 'field_encrypted' or 'volume_encrypted' alone triggers the finding if encryption_at_rest_enabled is false, meaning the declared method must be active and verified — not just configured in name.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Redis: check whether TLS is enforced and AUTH is required, and inspect whether application-level encryption is applied before writing tokens.
how_to_obtain.command: redis-cli -h <host> -p 6379 --tls INFO server | grep -E 'redis_version|tls' && redis-cli -h <host> ACL LIST
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of TLS config and ACL entries; absence of unencrypted plaintext token keys visible via 'KEYS session:*' sampling.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For PostgreSQL: query the column-level encryption configuration and check for pgcrypto or application-layer encryption on the session token column.
how_to_obtain.command: psql -U admin -d appdb -c "SELECT column_name, data_type FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'sessions' AND column_name ILIKE '%token%';" && psql -U admin -d appdb -c "SELECT token FROM sessions LIMIT 1;"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Token column values should appear as ciphertext or a fixed-length hash (e.g., base64-encoded blob), not a readable string. Data type 'bytea' or 'text' with non-human-readable content indicates encryption or hashing.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the application's session store configuration file or environment variables for field-level encryption library settings (e.g., AWS Encryption SDK, Fernet, or a KMS-backed cipher).
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rE 'encrypt|cipher|kms|fernet|token_secret' /app/config/ /etc/app/ ~/.env 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of a KMS key ARN, encryption key reference, or cipher algorithm string (e.g., AES-256-GCM) associated with the token storage field.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS-backed token stores (DynamoDB, RDS, ElastiCache), verify KMS encryption configuration via the AWS CLI.
how_to_obtain.command: aws rds describe-db-instances --query 'DBInstances[*].[DBInstanceIdentifier,StorageEncrypted,KmsKeyId]' --output table && aws elasticache describe-replication-groups --query 'ReplicationGroups[*].[ReplicationGroupId,AtRestEncryptionEnabled,TransitEncryptionEnabled]' --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: StorageEncrypted: true and a non-null KmsKeyId for RDS; AtRestEncryptionEnabled: true for ElastiCache.

typical_values: none (legacy or internal-only deployments with no data-at-rest requirements)
volume_encrypted (common in cloud-native deployments using EBS/RDS default KMS)
field_encrypted (less common; seen in high-compliance environments using application-layer encryption)
field_and_volume_encrypted (rare; found in PCI-DSS or government-regulated systems)

option_description: Indicates whether the logging framework or pipeline actively masks, redacts, or suppresses session token values before they are written to log storage or forwarded to downstream aggregators such as Splunk, ELK, CloudWatch Logs, or Datadog.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Token Exposure In Log And Audit Data' (score 5, medium criticality) when tokens_logged_in_plaintext is true and this attribute is false. Log pipelines typically have broader retention windows and weaker access controls than session stores, meaning an unmasked token value written to a log remains a live credential recoverable by any log consumer, backup operator, or SIEM analyst for the full log retention period.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the logging framework configuration for redaction or masking patterns targeting session token field names or bearer token formats.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rE 'mask|redact|obfuscat|session.token|bearer|Authorization' /app/config/logback.xml /etc/log4j2.xml /app/config/logging.yml 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A pattern such as '<maskPattern>session_token=[^&]+</maskPattern>' or a custom converter class reference indicates active masking.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Trigger a test authentication event and inspect the resulting log output to confirm token values do not appear in plaintext.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -X POST https://app/api/login -d '{"user":"testuser","pass":"testpass"}' && tail -n 50 /var/log/app/access.log | grep -iE 'token|session|bearer|auth'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log lines should show '***REDACTED***', '[MASKED]', or a truncated/hashed representation. Presence of full token strings (typically 32+ hex chars or JWT format) indicates masking is NOT active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk: navigate to Settings > Fields > Field Aliases or review the props.conf/transforms.conf for SEDCMD or REGEX-based token scrubbing rules. In Datadog: check Sensitive Data Scanner under Security > Configuration.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Settings > Data > Data Inputs > Search & Reporting > Review transforms.conf for SEDCMD targeting token patterns. Datadog: Security > Sensitive Data Scanner > Scanning Groups.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An active rule matching Bearer token patterns, session_id fields, or JWT regex (e.g., eyJ[A-Za-z0-9-_]+\.[A-Za-z0-9-_]+\.[A-Za-z0-9-_]+) with a REDACT or HASH action.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search historical log archives for JWT or session token patterns to determine whether past log writes contain unmasked tokens.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rE 'eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}|session_token=[A-Fa-f0-9]{32,}' /var/log/app/ 2>/dev/null | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No matches confirms effective masking. Any match indicates tokens have been logged in plaintext and masking is absent or incomplete.

typical_values: false (most common default; frameworks log full request/response objects without token awareness)
true (present in mature security programs with dedicated log scrubbing pipelines or DLP integration)

option_description: Describes the breadth of principals permitted to read log and audit data that may contain session token values, relative to the access controls applied to the session store itself. Values range from tightly restricted (matching session store ACLs) to fully unrestricted (publicly readable or broadly shared).
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Token Exposure In Log And Audit Data' when tokens_logged_in_plaintext is true and this value is 'broader_than_session_store' or 'unrestricted'. Even if tokens are not intentionally logged, this attribute determines the blast radius: if log consumers exceed session store principals, any token value that enters logs — via a debug statement, error trace, or serialization leak — is immediately accessible to a wider population than the protected store warrants.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate IAM principals with read access to the log storage bucket (S3) and compare against the principals with direct session store access.
how_to_obtain.command: aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket <log-bucket-name> | jq '.Policy | fromjson | .Statement[] | select(.Effect=="Allow") | {Principal, Action}' && aws rds describe-db-cluster-parameters --db-cluster-parameter-group-name <group> 2>/dev/null || echo 'Compare manually'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If the S3 bucket policy grants read to roles like 'DataAnalysts', 'SupportEngineers', or '*' that are absent from the session store IAM policy, the scope is 'broader_than_session_store' or 'unrestricted'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For CloudWatch Logs: list resource policies and log group permissions to determine who has GetLogEvents or FilterLogEvents access.
how_to_obtain.command: aws logs describe-resource-policies --output json | jq '.resourcePolicies[].policyDocument | fromjson' && aws logs describe-log-groups --log-group-name-prefix '/app/sessions' --query 'logGroups[*].logGroupName' --output text
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Resource policies or subscription filters referencing broad IAM roles or '*' principal indicate 'unrestricted' scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk: navigate to Settings > Access Controls > Roles and inspect which roles have access to the index containing application logs versus the index (if any) restricted to session data.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk Web: Settings > Access Controls > Roles > [role name] > Indexes searched by default. Compare roles with 'main' or 'app_logs' index access against roles restricted to 'session_store' index.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If roles such as 'splunk_user' or 'support_analyst' have access to app log indexes but not the session store, the scope is 'broader_than_session_store'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Elasticsearch/OpenSearch index-level access controls to compare who can read application log indices versus session data indices.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u elastic:<password> 'https://<es-host>:9200/_security/role' | jq '[to_entries[] | {role: .key, indices: .value.indices[].names}]' | grep -A2 'log\|session'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Roles with access to log indices but not session indices confirm 'broader_than_session_store'. Roles with no index restrictions confirm 'unrestricted'.

typical_values: broader_than_session_store (most common default; log platforms are shared across engineering, ops, and support teams)
unrestricted (observed in organizations without log access governance or using shared SIEM instances)
restricted_to_session_store_principals (rare; found only in high-maturity security programs with dedicated log segmentation)

option_description: An enumerated list of all database roles, IAM roles, or service accounts that hold SELECT/READ permissions on session token stores, including session tables, Redis key namespaces, and JWT blacklist stores. This is the factual access inventory used as input for access control policy evaluation.
security_impact: The Rego policy evaluates this list as the prerequisite for the 'Insufficient Access Control On Token Stores' exposure (score 5). A non-empty list combined with non_auth_roles_require_token_access being false triggers the finding unconditionally, and the absence of bulk read alerting compounds it. An accurate, complete enumeration is essential — undiscovered roles represent uncontrolled read paths to live credentials.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For PostgreSQL: enumerate all roles with SELECT privilege on the sessions table, including inherited grants.
how_to_obtain.command: psql -U admin -d appdb -c "SELECT grantee, privilege_type FROM information_schema.role_table_grants WHERE table_name = 'sessions' AND privilege_type = 'SELECT';" && psql -U admin -d appdb -c "\dp sessions"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A table listing role names (e.g., 'app_service', 'reporting_ro', 'dba_admin') with SELECT privilege. Each entry should be collected into the array.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Redis: list all ACL users and their command/key permissions to identify who can execute GET or SCAN on token namespaces.
how_to_obtain.command: redis-cli -h <host> -a <password> ACL LIST | grep -E 'GET|READ|SCAN|~session|~token|allkeys|allcommands'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each ACL entry showing ~session:* or allkeys with +GET or +SCAN represents a principal with token read access. Collect usernames into the array.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS IAM: identify all IAM roles and users with GetItem/Query/Scan permissions on the DynamoDB sessions table or with access to the RDS instance.
how_to_obtain.command: aws iam get-account-authorization-details --filter Role --output json | jq '[.RoleDetailList[] | select(.RolePolicyList[].PolicyDocument.Statement[].Action | tostring | test("dynamodb:GetItem|dynamodb:Scan|dynamodb:Query")) | .RoleName]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A JSON array of role names. Cross-reference against the sessions table ARN as the Resource to filter only those with actual token table access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For MySQL/MariaDB: query the grants system to find all accounts with SELECT on the session token table.
how_to_obtain.command: mysql -u root -p -e "SELECT User, Host FROM information_schema.USER_PRIVILEGES WHERE PRIVILEGE_TYPE='SELECT' UNION SELECT Grantee, '' FROM information_schema.TABLE_PRIVILEGES WHERE TABLE_NAME='user_sessions' AND PRIVILEGE_TYPE='SELECT';"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A result set of username@host entries. Any account not associated with the authentication service warrants justification review.

typical_values: ['app_auth_service', 'dba_admin'] (minimal, well-controlled)
['app_auth_service', 'app_worker', 'reporting_ro', 'dba_admin', 'legacy_etl_job'] (common over-provisioned state)
['root', 'app_service', 'analytics_user', 'support_tool'] (problematic; multiple non-auth principals with direct token access)

option_description: A boolean indicating whether every role listed in token_store_roles_with_read_access has a documented, function-necessary business justification for direct access to raw session token data. False means at least one role can read tokens without a clear functional requirement.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Insufficient Access Control On Token Stores' whenever token_store_roles_with_read_access is non-empty and this attribute is false — regardless of whether bulk read alerting is enabled. This condition directly models the principle of least privilege: roles such as reporting services, audit log writers, or batch workers that need session metadata (user ID, expiry time) do not require raw token values. Overly permissive access enables silent bulk extraction without triggering targeted alerts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review a data-access justification register, ITSM access request tickets, or system design documentation for each role identified in token_store_roles_with_read_access. Confirm whether each role's need for raw token data (not just session metadata) is explicitly documented.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Access Management system (e.g., Jira Service Management, ServiceNow): search for access request tickets referencing the session store or sessions table for each role. Review approval chain and stated business justification.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each role should have a ticket or design document stating WHY it needs SELECT on raw token values. Roles needing only user_id or session_expiry can access a restricted view. Any role without documented justification sets this attribute to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect application source code and configuration for roles that interact with the session store, and determine whether they read raw token values or only session metadata.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'SELECT.*token\|GET.*session\|find_by_token\|token_store.get' /app/src/ --include='*.py' --include='*.java' --include='*.go' --include='*.rb' | grep -v 'auth\|login\|validate\|verify'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Code paths accessing token values outside of authentication/validation modules (e.g., in reporting controllers, ETL scripts, or admin utilities) indicate roles without functional need for token data.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether non-auth roles are using database views or column-level permissions that restrict their access to metadata only, rather than raw token values.
how_to_obtain.command: psql -U admin -d appdb -c "\dv" | grep session && psql -U admin -d appdb -c "SELECT viewname, definition FROM pg_views WHERE viewname ILIKE '%session%';"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If reporting or worker roles access a view that excludes the token column (e.g., SELECT user_id, created_at, expires_at FROM sessions), their access may be justified. If they query the base table with the token column included, justification must be explicit.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the application and data teams to understand each non-auth role's actual use case, and verify that no role uses raw token values for purposes other than validation or revocation checking.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Schedule a 30-minute access review meeting with the application owner and DBA team. Ask: 'Does [role X] need to read the actual token string, or only session metadata such as user ID and expiry?'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A written record confirming each role's use case. Any role that cannot articulate a need for raw token bytes should have its access revoked or restricted via column-level permissions or views.

typical_values: false (most common; organizations rarely maintain formal data-access justification registers)
true (found in ISO 27001-certified or SOC 2 Type II environments with formal access review processes)

option_description: Indicates whether SIEM rules, database audit configurations, or cache monitoring are configured to detect and alert on bulk enumeration or mass extraction of session token store records — such as full-table scans, Redis KEYS * commands, or sustained high-volume GET patterns against token namespaces.
security_impact: The Rego policy uses this attribute as a compensating control in the 'Insufficient Access Control On Token Stores' evaluation: even when overly broad read access exists, active bulk-read alerting reduces the window for silent mass extraction. The finding is triggered both with and without this attribute when non_auth_roles_require_token_access is false, but absence of alerting represents an aggravated condition — an attacker with any token store read access can extract the full credential set without triggering a detection signal.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check PostgreSQL audit configuration (pgaudit) for rules that log or alert on sequential scans of the sessions table.
how_to_obtain.command: psql -U admin -d appdb -c "SHOW pgaudit.log;" && psql -U admin -d appdb -c "SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE query ILIKE '%SELECT%sessions%' AND state = 'active';"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: pgaudit.log should include 'read' to capture SELECT statements. Verify a downstream SIEM rule consumes pgaudit logs and alerts when SELECT count on 'sessions' exceeds a threshold (e.g., > 100 rows in 60 seconds).

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Redis: check keyspace notification settings and verify that a monitoring agent alerts on KEYS or SCAN commands against token namespaces.
how_to_obtain.command: redis-cli -h <host> CONFIG GET notify-keyspace-events && redis-cli -h <host> MONITOR 2>/dev/null | timeout 5 grep -iE 'KEYS|SCAN|HSCAN' || echo 'MONITOR check complete'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: notify-keyspace-events should be non-empty (e.g., 'KEA') to enable event tracking. MONITOR output showing KEYS * or SCAN 0 commands should be matched by an alert rule in the SIEM.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk SIEM: search for saved alert rules targeting high-volume token store queries. Navigate to Alerts and filter by index or sourcetype related to database or cache audit logs.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Search & Reporting > Alerts > (Filter by 'token' or 'session' keywords). Verify at least one active alert with a trigger condition such as 'count > 500 WHERE query contains sessions' within a 5-minute window.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An active alert with a cron schedule or real-time trigger, targeting a search like 'index=db_audit table=sessions action=SELECT | stats count | where count > 100'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query AWS CloudWatch for metric alarms or GuardDuty findings related to unusual DynamoDB scan activity on the sessions table.
how_to_obtain.command: aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --query 'MetricAlarms[?contains(AlarmName, `session`) || contains(AlarmName, `token`)].[AlarmName,StateValue,MetricName]' --output table && aws guardduty list-findings --detector-id <detector-id> --finding-criteria '{"Criterion":{"type":{"Eq":["UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/TorIPCaller"]}}}' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one CloudWatch alarm targeting DynamoDB ConsumedReadCapacityUnits or ScanReturnedItemCount with a threshold appropriate for token table size confirms alerting is active.

typical_values: false (default in most deployments; bulk read alerting requires deliberate SIEM tuning)
true (present in mature security operations with database activity monitoring tools such as Imperva, IBM Guardium, or custom SIEM rules)
null/unknown (common where no centralized SIEM is deployed or database audit logs are not forwarded)

option_description: Indicates whether a documented and actively enforced procedure exists for cryptographic erasure or secure deletion of session token data from decommissioned storage volumes, backup archives, and long-term retention datasets — including evidence of actual execution such as signed decommission checklists, automated pipeline confirmations, or audit trails.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Absent Or Non Compliant Disposal Procedure' (score 5) whenever this attribute is false. Policy documents alone without enforcement evidence do not satisfy the condition. Tokens recovered from improperly disposed backup media or snapshots may remain valid if revocation state is not independently maintained — creating a durable credential exposure window that survives the production session lifecycle. NIST SP 800-88 cryptographic erasure is the target standard.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request and review the data disposal or storage decommissioning runbook. Verify it explicitly addresses session token data, mandates NIST 800-88 compliant erasure for storage media, and requires sign-off evidence upon completion.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Locate in the internal wiki, GRC platform (e.g., Vanta, Drata, Archer), or IT asset management system. Search for 'media disposal', 'storage decommission', or 'data erasure' procedures. Confirm the procedure references session tokens or sensitive authentication data specifically.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A dated, versioned document with explicit steps for: (1) identifying token-bearing volumes/backups, (2) applying cryptographic erasure or DoD 5220.22-M/NIST 800-88 wipe, (3) obtaining sign-off from data owner and security team. Absence of any of these elements sets the attribute to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether automated backup lifecycle policies include secure deletion steps for RDS snapshots or S3 backup objects containing session data.
how_to_obtain.command: aws rds describe-db-cluster-snapshot-attributes --db-cluster-identifier <cluster-id> 2>/dev/null && aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket <backup-bucket> | jq '.Rules[] | {ID, Status, Expiration, NoncurrentVersionExpiration}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: S3 lifecycle rules showing Expiration with a defined day count AND a confirmation that deletion uses server-side encryption key deletion (not just object expiry) indicates automated enforcement. RDS snapshot deletion should be audited separately.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review audit trail records for recent storage decommission events to confirm the procedure has been executed and logged, not merely documented.
how_to_obtain.command: aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=DeleteDBSnapshot --start-time $(date -d '90 days ago' --iso-8601) | jq '.Events[] | {EventTime, Username, Resources}' && aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=DeleteObject --start-time $(date -d '90 days ago' --iso-8601) | jq '.Events[0:10]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: CloudTrail events showing DeleteDBSnapshot or DeleteObject actions correlated with decommission tickets confirm procedure execution. Absence of deletion events for volumes known to hold session backups indicates the procedure is not being enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the most recent completed decommission checklist or ITAM closure ticket for any storage asset that held session token data. Verify a cryptographic erasure confirmation signature exists.
how_to_obtain.navigation: ITSM (ServiceNow/Jira): search for closed 'storage decommission' tickets in the past 12 months. Filter by asset type = 'database' or 'backup volume'. Open the most recent and verify the checklist includes a 'secure erasure confirmed by:' field with a name, date, and method.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one completed ticket with a named approver, erasure method (e.g., 'AWS KMS key deletion + snapshot deletion confirmed'), and date within the past year. Policy without execution evidence returns false.

typical_values: false (most common; organizations define backup retention but rarely define cryptographic erasure on decommission)
true (present in PCI-DSS, HIPAA, or FedRAMP-regulated environments with formal media sanitization programs)

option_description: Indicates whether the authentication system maintains an independent, authoritative revocation registry — such as a Redis-backed denylist or database revocation table — that is consulted on every token validation request, independent of the token's own claims or expiry. This ensures that tokens recovered from improperly disposed or stolen media cannot be replayed even if they remain cryptographically valid.
security_impact: The Rego policy includes this attribute as a compensating control in the 'Absent Or Non Compliant Disposal Procedure' evaluation: when secure_deletion_procedure_defined is false, the absence of a separate revocation store compounds the risk by leaving recovered tokens without a runtime invalidation mechanism. Even with disposal procedures in place, stateless token validation (e.g., JWT signature-only verification) means a token extracted from a backup remains usable until its exp claim lapses — which may be hours, days, or indefinitely for tokens with no expiry.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether a Redis denylist or revocation key namespace exists and is populated with revoked token identifiers (JTI claims or session IDs).
how_to_obtain.command: redis-cli -h <host> -a <password> KEYS 'revoked:*' | head -20 && redis-cli -h <host> -a <password> DBSIZE && redis-cli -h <host> -a <password> TYPE revoked:$(redis-cli -h <host> KEYS 'revoked:*' | head -1 | awk '{print $1}')
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of 'revoked:*' keys with TTLs matching the maximum token lifetime confirms an active denylist. An empty keyspace or zero DBSIZE on the revocation namespace indicates no separate revocation store.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the application database for a token revocation or denylist table and verify it is being written to on logout/revocation events.
how_to_obtain.command: psql -U admin -d appdb -c "\dt *revok* *denylist* *blacklist* *invalid*" && psql -U admin -d appdb -c "SELECT COUNT(*), MAX(revoked_at) FROM token_revocations;" 2>/dev/null || echo 'Table not found'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A table (e.g., 'token_revocations', 'session_denylist') with recent rows and a MAX(revoked_at) timestamp within the expected session window confirms the store is active. 'Table not found' confirms the attribute is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect application source code or middleware configuration for token validation logic that checks a revocation store in addition to (or instead of) verifying the token's signature and claims.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'denylist\|revocation\|blacklist\|is_revoked\|check_revoked\|revocation_store' /app/src/ --include='*.py' --include='*.java' --include='*.go' --include='*.ts' | grep -v 'test\|spec\|mock'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Code in the token validation middleware (not just logout handlers) that performs a Redis GET or database SELECT against a revocation store before completing validation. Validation logic that only calls jwt.verify() or checks exp/nbf claims without a denylist lookup confirms false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test the revocation mechanism by revoking a test token and then attempting to use it: if the API returns 401 Unauthorized immediately (not waiting for natural expiry), a separate revocation state store is confirmed active.
how_to_obtain.command: TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST https://app/api/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"user":"testuser","pass":"testpass"}' | jq -r '.token') && curl -s -X POST https://app/api/logout -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" && curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -X GET https://app/api/profile -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HTTP 401 response after logout confirms revocation state is checked independently. HTTP 200 response confirms that revocation is NOT enforced at validation time — the token remains valid based on its claims alone.

typical_values: false (default for JWT-based systems where stateless validation is the design intent)
true (present in systems using opaque session tokens checked against a session store, or JWT systems with explicit denylist middleware)
false (common in microservice architectures where each service validates tokens independently without a shared revocation feed)
